sections.guidingQuestion: What must happen before two daughter cells inherit complete copies of a chromosome?
sections.explanation:
Replication precedes cell division because each daughter cell requires an inherited copy of the DNA base sequence. Accurate sequence copying allows the new cells in a growing root, a healing wound or a dividing bacterium to retain the genetic instructions of the parent cell. It does not mean that replication is perfectly error-free; rare mistakes can persist as mutations.

The DNA sequence serves as an ordered template. Replication copies the whole DNA molecule; transcription later uses selected DNA regions to produce RNA. Keeping these processes distinct explains how a cell can preserve genes while changing which genes it expresses.

Follow the consequence: an unreplicated chromosome contains one DNA double helix; a correctly replicated chromosome contains two identical sister chromatids. Copying sequence information first makes it possible for division to supply each future daughter nucleus with the same instructions. In an ordinary cell cycle this copying occurs during S phase, before mitosis—not during cytokinesis.
sections.revisionSummary: Replication precedes cell division because each daughter cell requires an inherited copy of the DNA base sequence. The DNA sequence serves as an ordered template.
sections.workedExample: A skin basal cell duplicates its genomic DNA before mitosis so its daughters can continue producing skin tissue.

sections.guidingQuestion: After semi-conservative replication, each daughter DNA duplex contains which strands?
sections.explanation:
The two parental DNA strands separate. Each becomes a template for synthesis of a complementary new strand, producing two double helices that each contain one original strand and one newly made strand. This arrangement is called semi-conservative, not conservative or dispersive.

A pairs with T and G pairs with C in DNA. When a template exposes a base, the matching incoming deoxyribonucleotide can pair at that position. Enzyme selectivity and later proofreading further increase fidelity: complementary pairing alone is not an absolute guarantee against mistakes.

A template strand does not dictate where its own bases remain; it determines the order of incoming complementary nucleotides. Separating the two parental strands therefore produces two templates, each leading to one parental-plus-new double helix. A pairs with T and G with C. The rule strongly supports accuracy but does not make errors impossible.

sections.guidingQuestion: What is the immediate action of helicase at a replication fork?
sections.explanation:
Helicase uses energy to unwind the parental double helix and disrupt the hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, exposing the two template strands. The sugar–phosphate backbones remain intact at the fork; helicase does not cut the strands into nucleotides.

DNA polymerase selects incoming deoxyribonucleotides against the DNA template and catalyses phosphodiester-bond formation in the growing strand. In ordinary cellular replication it extends an existing primer rather than starting a strand from nothing. Its accuracy depends on base selection and, for proofreading polymerases, exonuclease activity.

Helicase disrupts hydrogen bonds between paired bases without cutting the sugar–phosphate backbone. Exposed parental strands are templates; DNA polymerase selects matching DNA nucleotides and makes covalent phosphodiester links in the growing daughter chain. Helicase and polymerase carry out different chemical tasks.

sections.guidingQuestion: Which sequence of conditions describes one ordinary PCR cycle?
sections.explanation:
A PCR cycle first heats DNA to separate strands, then lowers the temperature so short DNA primers can anneal to complementary sequences on opposite strands, then allows thermostable Taq DNA polymerase to extend those primers. The chosen primers define the target; repeated cycles can produce many copies of the region. PCR is not the same as replication of an entire chromosome.

Negatively charged DNA migrates toward the positive electrode through a gel under an electric field. Under comparable conditions, shorter DNA fragments generally travel farther through the gel. DNA ladders supply reference fragment lengths; a band position is evidence about fragment size, not by itself the complete nucleotide sequence.

Temperature makes three different things possible in successive PCR stages: high heat separates template strands, cooling allows short primers to anneal to flanking complementary sites, and extension at the polymerase's working temperature copies the bounded region. Taq polymerase is heat-stable. In agarose gel electrophoresis, negatively charged DNA migrates toward the positive electrode; with an appropriate gel and conditions, smaller fragments generally travel farther.

sections.guidingQuestion: Why are several independent DNA markers used in forensic profiling?
sections.explanation:
Forensic investigations and parentage testing compare informative DNA markers. Amplification makes small samples analysable and gel or capillary separation distinguishes fragment-length patterns. Agreement at one marker is weak evidence; combining multiple independent markers can greatly reduce the chance of a coincidental match.

A DNA profile is evidence to be interpreted with sample integrity, contamination controls, population frequencies and a documented chain of custody. A match does not prove when or how biological material arrived at a scene, nor does a paternity result identify a person using one band alone.

A matching DNA-band or STR profile is evidence of consistency with a sample source, not a proof that excludes contamination, relatives or procedural error. More independently selected markers usually decrease the probability of a coincidental match. Interpretation depends on sample handling, population frequencies, and a defensible statistical model; biological relatedness complicates paternity and forensic comparisons.

Matching loci supports a probabilistic comparison, not the claim that two people must be identical. Testing more independently informative STR markers generally reduces the chance of a coincidental profile match. Contamination, sample quality and population assumptions still matter. Illustrative classroom comparisons must not be presented as observed forensic case data.

sections.guidingQuestion: At which end can DNA polymerase add the next nucleotide?
sections.explanation:
A DNA strand has chemically different 5′ and 3′ ends because nucleotides have a phosphate-linked 5′ carbon and a hydroxyl-bearing 3′ carbon. The two template strands in a duplex run antiparallel. DNA polymerase attaches an incoming nucleotide's 5′ phosphate to the free 3′ hydroxyl of the growing strand; every new DNA strand therefore elongates 5′→3′.

As polymerase extends new DNA in the 5′→3′ direction, it reads the complementary template in the 3′→5′ direction. An arrow in a diagram must identify whether it shows fork motion, template direction or strand elongation; these are not interchangeable.

The phosphate of an incoming dNTP attaches to the free 3′-OH of the nascent chain, so elongation is always 5′→3′. Polymerase reads its template antiparallel, 3′→5′. Mark both directions separately on a diagram; reversing the fork direction changes which template is leading, never the chemical direction of polymerization.

DNA polymerase extends a DNA strand only 5′→3′ by attaching each incoming nucleotide to the available 3′ end. Its template is read in the antiparallel 3′→5′ direction. For a template 3′–TACG–5′, the daughter sequence is 5′–ATGC–3′. The incoming nucleotide contributes its 5′ phosphate to the new phosphodiester linkage; the direction arrow describes strand growth, not fork movement.

misconceptions.correction: Both leading and lagging products are always synthesized 5′→3′.

As polymerase extends new DNA in the 5′→3′ direction, it reads the complementary template in the 3′→5′ direction. An arrow in a diagram must identify whether it shows fork motion, template direction or strand elongation; these are not interchangeable.

The phosphate of an incoming dNTP attaches to the free 3′-OH of the nascent chain, so elongation is always 5′→3′. Polymerase reads its template antiparallel, 3′→5′. Mark both directions separately on a diagram; reversing the fork direction changes which template is leading, never the chemical direction of polymerization.

teachingBlocks.title: Keep both DNA strand directions explicit
teachingBlocks.explanation: DNA polymerase extends a DNA strand only 5′→3′ by attaching each incoming nucleotide to the available 3′ end. Its template is read in the antiparallel 3′→5′ direction. For a template 3′–TACG–5′, the daughter sequence is 5′–ATGC–3′. The incoming nucleotide contributes its 5′ phosphate to the new phosphodiester linkage; the direction arrow describes strand growth, not fork movement.

sections.guidingQuestion: What distinguishes the newly synthesized lagging strand from the leading strand?
sections.explanation:
On the leading-strand template, a newly primed strand is extended continuously in the same overall direction in which the replication fork opens. Because the polymerase can only extend a 3′ end, the leading template is read 3′→5′ toward the fork.

The opposing lagging template has the reverse polarity, so short RNA primers must be placed repeatedly on newly exposed DNA. Each Okazaki fragment is extended 5′→3′ away from the advancing fork. Fragment synthesis is discontinuous, even though the finished lagging daughter strand becomes one continuous DNA molecule after primer replacement and ligation.

At a fork travelling right, a 3′→5′ template oriented left-to-right can be copied toward the fork continuously; its opposing 5′→3′ template needs repeated primers and short fragments made away from the fork. Okazaki fragments are eventually joined into a continuous daughter molecule. Both strands still elongate 5′→3′.

sections.guidingQuestion: In bacterial DNA replication, which enzyme mainly extends new DNA from RNA primers?
sections.explanation:
In the prokaryotic system specified by the guide, primase makes short RNA primers that provide the free 3′ end needed by DNA polymerase III. Polymerase III extends the DNA segment while reading the parental template. Leading synthesis typically needs one initiation at a fork; lagging synthesis needs a fresh primer for each fragment.

DNA polymerase I removes RNA primers and replaces them with DNA. DNA ligase then seals remaining nicks in the sugar–phosphate backbone, creating continuous DNA. The enzyme numbers refer to bacterial polymerases; do not automatically transplant this division of labour to eukaryotic replication.

In the prokaryotic model required here, primase synthesizes RNA primers because polymerases need an existing 3′-OH. DNA polymerase III extends the primers with DNA, polymerase I removes RNA primer nucleotides and replaces them with DNA, and ligase seals remaining nicks between adjacent DNA fragments. Distinguish replacement of a primer from sealing a phosphodiester-bond discontinuity.

In the prescribed prokaryotic model, primase synthesizes RNA primers, DNA polymerase III extends DNA and proofreads, DNA polymerase I replaces RNA primers with DNA, and DNA ligase seals the remaining backbone nicks. These polymerase I/III names should not be presented as the enzyme names for eukaryotic replication.

sections.guidingQuestion: Which activity directly removes a mismatched terminal nucleotide during bacterial polymerase III proofreading?
sections.explanation:
Bacterial DNA polymerase III tests the terminal base pair while the daughter strand is being extended. If the 3′ end carries an incorrectly matched nucleotide, its 3′→5′ exonuclease activity removes that terminal nucleotide and the polymerase incorporates the properly matched replacement.

DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to an existing correctly paired 3′ end. An incorrect terminal base makes the extension less favourable, permitting transfer to the proofreading site. This is a correction during replication; separate post-replication DNA repair pathways can also remove errors, but are not identical to polymerase III proofreading.

DNA polymerase III may pause when a just-added base is mismatched; its 3′→5′ exonuclease removes the incorrectly paired terminal nucleotide. Polymerization can then resume with the correct nucleotide at the 3′ end. This proofreading lowers error frequency; repair systems may act later, and replication fidelity is high but not absolute.

questions.prompt: Using a suitable biological context, explain replication in DNA replication and correct this claim: "Replication makes RNA copies for translation."
questions.answer: Replication precedes cell division because each daughter cell requires an inherited copy of the DNA base sequence. Accurate sequence copying allows the new cells in a growing root, a healing wound or a dividing bacterium to retain the genetic instructions of the parent cell. It does not mean that replication is perfectly error-free; rare mistakes can persist as mutations. Replication produces new DNA molecules; transcription produces RNA. A skin basal cell duplicates its genomic DNA before mitosis so its daughters can continue producing skin tissue.
markingPoints: Follow the consequence: an unreplicated chromosome contains one DNA double helix; a correctly replicated chromosome contains two identical sister chromatids
Copying sequence information first makes it possible for division to supply each future daughter nucleus with the same instructions
Correct the common inference: Replication produces new DNA molecules; transcription produces RNA.

questions.answer: The two parental DNA strands separate. Each becomes a template for synthesis of a complementary new strand, producing two double helices that each contain one original strand and one newly made strand. This arrangement is called semi-conservative, not conservative or dispersive. Each daughter duplex contains one original and one newly synthesized strand. For a short template 3′-TACG-5′, the new antiparallel DNA strand is 5′-ATGC-3′.

questions.prompt: Using a suitable biological context, explain proofreading in DNA replication and correct this claim: "Proofreading removes a base from the middle of the parental template as the normal first step."
questions.answer: Bacterial DNA polymerase III tests the terminal base pair while the daughter strand is being extended. If the 3′ end carries an incorrectly matched nucleotide, its 3′→5′ exonuclease activity removes that terminal nucleotide and the polymerase incorporates the properly matched replacement. Polymerase III removes a mismatched newly added 3′ terminal nucleotide and replaces it with the correct one. If a new G is paired opposite template G by mistake, polymerase III can excise terminal G and insert the complementary C.
markingPoints: DNA polymerase III may pause when a just-added base is mismatched; its 3′→5′ exonuclease removes the incorrectly paired terminal nucleotide
Polymerization can then resume with the correct nucleotide at the 3′ end
Correct the common inference: Polymerase III removes a mismatched newly added 3′ terminal nucleotide and replaces it with the correct one.

questions.prompt: An idealized PCR model begins with 20 amplifiable target duplexes and assumes perfect doubling per cycle. Calculate the expected count after four cycles, then explain why a real reaction may produce fewer copies.
questions.answer: 20 × 2⁴ = 320 target duplexes in this idealized model. Actual reaction efficiency can be reduced by reagent limitations, incomplete primer annealing or inhibition; amplification will not always double perfectly.
markingPoints: Correct multiplication 20 × 2⁴ = 320 duplexes.
One valid mechanism that prevents perfect exponential efficiency.
